items.text: Assignment statement: the statement variable = expression; which stores a data-type value in a variable.

The left-hand side must be a single variable. The right-hand side can be any expression whose type is compatible with the variable's type. = is not mathematical equality (a + b = b + a and 1 = a are illegal).

First the right-hand side is fully evaluated using the variables' current values (left to right). Then that value is stored in the left-hand variable, replacing its old value, and execution moves to the next statement.
As a statement it prints nothing; its result is the new value of the left variable (after c = a + b; with a = 1234 and b = 99, c is 1333). Used as an expression, its value is the value assigned.
Exactly one variable, the left one, changes, and its old value is lost. Variables on the right keep their values: x = x + 5; with x = 5 makes x 10.
The left side must be a declared variable whose type accepts the value. Assignment is how that variable's value changes.
A declaration can include the first assignment (int x = 5;). Assigning to a variable that was never declared does not compile.
Exchanging a[i] and a[j] takes three assignments in a fixed order through a temporary, because each assignment overwrites its target.
int t = a; a = b; b = t; works only in this order, because every assignment destroys its left variable's old value.
x op= e is shorthand for x = x op e. The left variable's current value is fetched first and then combined with e.
Because an assignment is an expression whose value is the value stored, and = groups right to left, a = b = 0 first stores 0 in b and then stores that 0 in a.

Using a double as a for-loop index is legal but bad practice: the number of iterations depends on an equality test between double values, which may not give the result you expect.
Identity: an array access expression; a[i] names the single element variable at position i of the array a refers to.
Declarative: the index is any int-valued expression in square brackets; the valid indices of an array of length n are 0 to n-1, and an access outside that range throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

Sequencing: the array reference is evaluated before the index; the index expression is fully evaluated with current variable values; the bounds are checked; then the element is fetched or, on the left of =, becomes the target. In a[i] = a[j], the target a[i] is located before a[j] is read.
Result: a[i] has the element type and the value currently stored at position i. For int[] a = {5, 7, 9}, a[1] is 7 and a[0] + a[2] is 14.
State transition: reading a[i] changes nothing. a[i] = v changes only element i (i, a and all other elements are unchanged), and a[i]++ adds 1 to that one element.
An element can be indexed only after the array is created, and the n given to new sets the valid indices 0..n-1.
A traversal uses the loop variable as the index, so the same expression a[i] reaches a different element on each pass.
Every index value is checked against 0 and a.length at run time; any other value throws.
a[i] on a 2-D array yields row i (itself a 1-D array), and a[i][j] then indexes into that row.
The exchange reads and writes elements only through their indices: t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t.
A lookup table uses a data value as the index (months[m]), so the data must lie in 0..length-1.
Indices start at 0, so the last element is a[N-1]; misreading this convention is the usual source of off-by-one errors.
Plan/role: random access, reaching any element directly by its position in constant time (address plus index), so code touches only the elements it needs.

Conservation: changing the index expression (i to i+1 or i-1) shifts which element is touched and can leave the bounds at the ends. Writing a[a[i]] instead of a[i] uses an element value as the index, a different access entirely. Changing what is stored never changes the positions.

Applicability: index when you need a particular element by position, or when the position is computed from data (counts[score]++, months[m]). When every value is processed in order and the position is never needed, an enhanced for loop is simpler.

rule broken: The index must be in 0..a.length-1. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: index < 0 or >= a.length, e.g. a[a.length], a[i+1] on the last pass, a[i-1] at i = 0, a[0] of an empty array (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException)
